title: Securing Local-Area Networks in AI Supercomputing Data Centers
content: Artificial-intelligence supercomputers concentrate high-value training data, model weights, credentials, accelerators, and orchestration services behind extremely fast local networks. Their security problem differs from that of a conventional office LAN because several fabrics coexist: out-of-band management, in-band services, storage, and high-performance compute communication. This survey synthesizes standards, government guidance, vendor reference architectures, and peer-reviewed systems-security research to examine how those fabrics change the attack surface. The review finds that segmentation, zero-trust access, strong device and workload identity, encrypted management, secure firmware, and independent recovery paths form a consistent baseline. However, high-performance mechanisms such as InfiniBand and Remote Direct Memory Access create residual risks because isolation identifiers are not necessarily cryptographic protections, one-sided operations can bypass host processing, and monitoring at accelerator-fabric rates is difficult. The paper proposes a cross-plane control model that binds job identity to network authorization and data provenance, then identifies research priorities in line-rate cryptography, revocable RDMA capabilities, DPU assurance, AI-aware telemetry, and disruption-tolerant containment. The resulting view treats LAN security as a property of the complete AI workload lifecycle rather than as a perimeter firewall problem.
